Subject: Quick follow-up + proposed next steps from today's demo

Hi Claire and Raj,

Thanks again for the time today — really helpful to see the workflow you use for patient-summary generation. Quick recap and the asks we committed to: 

1) Top pain you raised: intermittent partial outputs when streaming long summaries (sentences cut off mid-thought), which causes downstream truncation in your ingestion pipeline.
2) Quality/regression concern: you observed some hallucination spikes vs your current baseline on medication lists and dates.
3) Next steps we promised: provide candidate models + guidance on stop-token/stop-sequence behavior, share a prompt-set you can run locally, and a short latency/throughput estimate for streaming at your target QPS.

I've attached the prompt-set we discussed (meddata-example-prompts.txt) and a short snippet file with the stop-sequence experiments we ran (streaming-stopseq-snippets.txt).

Can you confirm the two priority evaluation axes for you: (A) coherence at streaming checkpoints (2–4s windows) and (B) hallucination rate on structured fields (medications, dates)? If we’re aligned, I’ll ask Rishi to produce a short model recommendation matrix + suggested eval harness and a small test run against one of your representative prompts.

Proposed timeline:
- Today (EOD): confirm priority axes + share any additional representative prompts you want included
- Tue 2027-04-06: Redwood delivers model suggestions + sample eval results (1–2 prompts, 1k tokens each)
- Wed 2027-04-07: sync to review results and decide on pilot scope

Thanks — we want to make sure streaming UX issues are addressed before a pilot so your ingestion doesn't have to special-case partial sentences.

Best,
Neha Kapoor

Neha — thanks for the quick summary and for sending the prompts. A few clarifications from our side: 

- Priority axes: yes, exactly the two you listed. In particular, the streaming checkpoints matter because we buffer partial outputs into our audit trail. If the model stops mid-sentence, the downstream matcher flags a false positive and a human has to fix it.
- Example prompts: I attached a short file (I can share if helpful) with three real examples from production — one is a 900-token case note that typically takes ~3.2s on our current infra.
- Concern: we saw behavior where the model emits the stop-sequence token but then continues producing another short clause (looks like a soft-stop). That causes our splitter to glue fragments together incorrectly. Can Redwood quantify how often that happens or recommend a robust stop policy?

Also: we're sensitive to latency spikes. Your hosted API would be used for the pilot; what should we expect at the 95th percentile for streaming latency at ~12 concurrent streams at 1–2 TPS each?

Happy to jump on a quick technical call if that helps.

—Claire
Claire Chen

Team / Claire — quick summary of what I ran this morning and recommended options. See attached summary spreadsheet (benchmarks-summary-20270402.xlsx).

Key findings (200 runs per prompt, mixed lengths 200–1k tokens):
- Candidate A (redwood/phoenix-7b-quant): quantized 8-bit, cost-efficient. Observed soft-stop rate: 6.5% (i.e., stop token emitted then extra 1–6 characters in 200 runs). Typical p95 streaming latency at 12 concurrent streams: ~360ms additional time per checkpoint (end-to-end p95 2.9s for a 3.2s baseline).
- Candidate B (redwood/aurora-13b-fp16): higher-quality option. Soft-stop rate: 1.1% across runs. p95 streaming latency at 12 concurrent streams: ~420ms (end-to-end p95 3.1s).

Interpretation: the soft-stop phenomenon correlates with early termination heuristics in the tokenizer + sequence boundary handling in the runtime. Higher model precision reduces frequency but doesn't eliminate it. For strict stop guarantees we recommend either: 
  a) explicit post-stream sanitization (simple rule: drop trailing fragment after last full stop or known delimiter), or
  b) inject explicit stop-token sequences in the prompt and run a brief streaming post-check to trim characters after the stop token.

Prompt engineering suggestions we tested (included in meddata-example-prompts.txt):
- Add an explicit suffix: "\n\n-- END SUMMARY --" and use that exact delimiter as a stop token. This reduced soft-stop cases by ~60% in Candidate B and ~45% in Candidate A.
- Limit max_new_tokens to 512 for long-case notes and prefer a conservative temperature (0.0–0.3) to reduce trailing fragments.

Artifacts attached: benchmarks-summary-20270402.xlsx (summary + per-run CSV sheets), streaming-stopseq-snippets.txt (representative transcripts).

Pilot recommendation: start with Candidate B for a 2-week pilot (better quality + lower hallucination on structured fields) but configure a stop-token suffix and run the sanitization pass client-side. If cost is a primary constraint, Candidate A with stricter prompt suffixing + sanitization is acceptable.

Proposed next actions:
- Neha: share the pilot scope and finalize which customer prompts to include (EOD Tue 2027-04-06)
- Claire: confirm you want Candidate B as the pilot model or ask for the lower-cost Candidate A
- Marissa: I can hand the artifacts to you for SOW/technical onboarding notes once Claire confirms

Happy to jump on a 30m call if you want me to walk through the workbook.

—Rishi
